section_summaries.epidemiology: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP), caused by the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii, is an acute, potentially life-threatening pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals. In tropical countries, most adult patients with PCP have AIDS, while in developed countries, it also affects patients receiving chemotherapy or immunosuppressants, and infants with kwashiorkor. Early reports from developing regions showed 3%-35% prevalence, but more recently, 45%-65% has been reported among AIDS patients with respiratory symptoms, possibly due to differences in study design, prophylaxis rates, and diagnostic sensitivity. In developed countries, PCP incidence has significantly declined with antiretroviral therapy (ART) and Pneumocystis prophylaxis, a trend expected in developing regions with increased ART use. Most PCP cases worldwide in HIV-infected people occur when CD4 counts fall below 200 cells/mm³.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: P. jirovecii can reside latently in the alveolar septal walls of asymptomatic individuals. Immunodeficiency is the primary predisposing condition for pneumonia, though newly acquired organisms can also cause disease. The organism causes denudation of alveolar cells, leading to characteristic foamy, honeycombed intra-alveolar exudates of cysts and desquamated alveolar cells, with an interstitial infiltrate of plasma cells and lymphocytes. As pneumonia progresses, the number of organisms increases, resulting in diffuse pneumonitis. Systemic dissemination is rare but can occur with aerosolized pentamidine, potentially involving the liver, spleen, lymph nodes, or bone marrow. The level of immunodeficiency for PCP onset in developing regions mirrors that in high-income countries.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: PCP can manifest with acute or gradual onset, being more fulminant in HIV-negative patients. Common symptoms (80-100% of cases) include fever, non-productive or minimally productive cough (95-100%), and dyspnea (95%), typically progressing over 1-2 weeks, often accompanied by fatigue, chest pain, and weight loss. Physical examination may reveal tachypnea with bibasilar rales or a normal lung exam. Extrapulmonary pneumocystosis can cause lymph node, spleen, or liver enlargement. Oxygen saturation is low at rest and declines with exertion; arterial oxygen tension (PaO2) is low, carbon dioxide is normal, and the alveolar-arterial (A-a) gradient is increased. Chest x-rays are initially normal in up to one-fourth of patients but later evolve into bilateral, diffuse, interstitial infiltrates, especially in the lower lung fields. Variant findings include upper lobe involvement, focal consolidation, or thin-walled cavities (pneumatoceles) that may cause pneumothorax. High-resolution CT scans can show patchy or nodular ground-glass attenuation. Lactic dehydrogenase (LDH) levels are often elevated. In developing countries, PCP is often recognized at a more severe stage, characterized by high respiratory rates (30-80 per minute) and very low O2 saturation (60%-82%).
section_summaries.diagnosis: PCP diagnosis requires confirmation by obtaining a respiratory specimen, as clinical and radiographic features overlap with other community-acquired pneumonias. Empiric anti-pneumocystis treatment should be initiated while awaiting diagnostic results. Gallium-67 citrate scanning and serum beta-D-glucan assays have limited utility due to lack of specificity or availability. Respiratory specimens can be induced using a handheld nebulizer with hypertonic saline. Staining methods include silver nitrate, toluidine blue O, or Giemsa stain. Indirect immunofluorescence or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for P. jirovecii can also be performed, though PCR can detect colonization, so quantitative PCR assays may be preferred to distinguish disease from colonization. Sputum induction sensitivity ranges from 55% to 92%. If sputum is negative, bronchoalveolar lavage is performed. Lung biopsy is not required. Non-invasive tests like oropharyngeal washes combined with PCR are effective diagnostic methods in resource-limited settings.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment regimens for PCP in industrialized countries are applicable globally. Illness severity determines whether oral or intravenous regimens are used. For mild to moderate disease (PO2 >70, A-a gradient <35 mmO2), a 3-week oral course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) (15 mg TMP/kg/day in three divided doses) is the preferred regimen. Adverse effects of TMP-SMX include rash, cytopenias, and gastrointestinal upset. Alternatives for patients with non-life-threatening rash include trimethoprim plus dapsone, atovaquone, or primaquine plus clindamycin. Severe disease (PO2 <70; A-a gradient >35 mmO2) requires intravenous TMP-SMX. If intolerant or unresponsive to TMP-SMX after 7 days, intravenous pentamidine isethionate (3 mg/kg/day) can be given, but it has more serious side effects. Adjunctive corticosteroids (prednisone 40 mg twice daily for days 1-5, then tapered) initiated within 24-72 hours of anti-pneumocystis therapy prevent early oxygenation deterioration in severe cases. Mortality rates in low-income regions (10%-27%) are similar to the United States, but higher in children (10%-80%), possibly due to late treatment initiation or lack of ART.
section_summaries.prevention: Prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) reduces PCP incidence in people with AIDS and CD4 cell counts below 200 cells/mm³. Prophylaxis can be discontinued when CD4 cell counts remain above 200 cells/mm³ for more than 3 months.
